The new chapter opens with “Alif-Lãm-Mĩm,” three separate letters rather than an ordinary sentence. Their placement calls the reader to pause before the declaration about Allah that follows in the next verse. The letters are part of the Quran’s own speech, yet their full meaning is not set out in the verse itself. This teaches a beginning marked by attention and humility: a person can recognise the letters, recite them, and still know that Allah knows more than the reader does. The letters are not an empty sound placed before the message. They stand at the beginning of a chapter that will speak about Allah’s oneness, revelation, earlier Books, guidance, knowledge, and the right way to respond to clear and elusive verses. They also remind the reader that the Quran is made of the same letters people use in their own speech, while its guidance and power to bring a like book remain beyond human ability. The passage before it ended with a prayer for Allah’s help and mercy. This opening begins the next chapter by putting the reader before words whose full depth belongs to Allah, then immediately directs attention to the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining Lord. The right response is neither to claim certainty where the verse has not given it nor to turn the unknown into a reason to ignore what is clear. It is to listen, receive the Book, and allow the clear guidance that follows to shape belief and action.

The verse begins the chapter’s central declaration about Allah. “Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining” rules out every rival in worship. It does not simply say that Allah is greater than other powers. It states that nothing else has the right to receive the submission, dependence, and devotion that belong to Allah. The words “the Ever-Living” name life that does not begin, weaken, or end as created life does. Every creature lives by a life given to it and can lose it; Allah’s life is not received from another. The words “All-Sustaining” name the One who exists by Himself and sustains all that exists. Creation depends upon Him for being, provision, and continuance, while He depends on none of it. The two names give the reason for the declaration at the start: the One who lives perfectly and sustains all things is the only One worthy of worship. The verse echoes the great declaration near the end of the previous chapter, but it now begins a new passage about revelation and the Books Allah has sent. The reader is not asked to treat revelation as detached information. It comes from the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining Lord who alone deserves worship and whose knowledge and power will be described in the verses that follow.

**No god worthy of worship.**

In the words (Allah: there is no god but He) which follow immediately, the doctrine of the Oneness of Allah has been put forth as a categorical declaration. It means that there is absolutely nothing worthy of worship other than Allah. Therefore, it is crystal clear that all things in this world which have no power to come into being by themselves, nor can they sustain it - be they idols carved in stone, or water, or trees, or angels and apostles - none of them is worthy of worship. The only Being worthy of worship is the One who has always been Alive and Present and shall always live and sustain. (Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists) and,. (Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive) Who dies not and is not evanescent, (the Eternal) the Self-subsistent Who has no beginning. Allah is the One Who alone deserves to be worshipped.

The only Being worthy of worship is the One who has always been Alive and Present and shall always live and sustain. (Allah! The verse turns from the Lord who alone deserves worship to the Book He has sent. “He has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book in truth” describes the Quran as revelation from Allah, not a message made by human invention or guesswork. Truth belongs to what it brings, what it teaches, and the One who sent it. “Confirming what came before it” places the Quran within a line of earlier revelation rather than presenting it as a message cut off from all that came before. It confirms the truth Allah sent to earlier prophets and the central call to worship Him alone. “As He revealed the Torah and the Gospel” names two earlier Books given before the Quran. Their mention shows that Allah’s guidance did not begin with the final Book or with one people alone. The verse follows the declaration that Allah is the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining and prepares the next verse’s description of revelation as guidance and a standard between truth and falsehood. The same Lord who sustains creation has sent guidance through Books and messengers. The reader is therefore asked to see revelation as a coherent gift from Allah across time, while receiving the Quran as the Book revealed in truth. The verse does not erase the particular role of the Quran; it names its confirmation of what was true in earlier revelation and sets it within the continuing guidance of Allah.

This verse completes the description of revelation by giving its purpose and the consequence of rejecting it. “Previously, as a guide for people” returns to the Torah and Gospel named before it and describes them as guidance from Allah. Guidance is not limited to a private feeling; it directs people away from error and toward what is right. “And ˹also˺ revealed the Standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺” names the standard that separates truth from falsehood, guidance from misguidance, and what is right from what is corrupt. The Book does not leave every claim equal or every path uncertain. “Surely those who reject Allah’s revelations will suffer a severe torment” gives the warning for refusing the signs Allah has sent. The danger is not only a failure to understand a difficult point. It is a rejection of Allah’s guidance after it has been made known. “For Allah is Almighty, capable of punishment” closes with power and justice. No one can prevent Allah from bringing about what He has promised, and His punishment is not a powerless threat. The verse follows the statement that the Quran confirms earlier Books, so the standard is not set against the reality of revelation. It clarifies the truth sent through it. The reader is called to receive guidance as a mercy and to recognise that rejecting Allah’s signs has a serious end because the One who revealed them is Almighty and able to requite. The standard is therefore not a human preference that changes whenever a claim is forceful or popular. It is revelation from Allah, sent as guidance and as a means of recognising truth. The warning gives the standard seriousness, while Allah’s might assures the reader that guidance and justice do not depend on human power alone.

5.text:
The verse gives a short statement with a complete scope: “Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah.” It reaches every place a person can see and every place beyond human sight. Nothing in the earth is too small, buried, private, or distant from His knowledge. Nothing in the heavens is too high or remote. The verse follows the warning to people who reject Allah’s revelations and prepares the description of Allah shaping people in the wombs. His knowledge is not limited to public actions or outward form. It includes what is open and what is hidden, what has occurred and what a person cannot reach. This knowledge gives the foundation for guidance and judgment. A human being knows only part of a situation and often discovers what was hidden too late. Allah knows the whole of creation and each person within it. The verse therefore calls the reader to honesty before Allah and trust in His guidance. No secret removes a person from His knowledge, but no need or difficulty is hidden from Him either. The next verse gives one close sign of that knowledge and power in the shaping of every person before birth.

**Nothing hidden from Allah.**

Nothing no existent thing whatever is hidden in heaven and earth from God on account of His knowledge of universals and particulars. Truly, nothing is hidden from Allah, in the earth or in the heaven He it is Who shapes you in the wombs as He wills. Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. He knows everything, whether it is open or hidden. A servant does not breathe a single breath without God counting it muḥṣīhi.

**Earth, heavens, and creation.**

Nothing no existent thing whatever is hidden in heaven and earth from God on account of His knowledge of universals and particulars. God specifies them heaven and earth because sensory perception does not go beyond these. Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. Not a particle exists in the heaven and earth unless He is its originator and creator mubdiʿ hi. The right course of action for man can be determined only by a Being who has not only known man from his birth to his death, but also knows what has gone before his birth and what will happen after his death. It is, therefore, only God who, after placing the nature of man in the perspective of the entire universe, may decree what kind of conduct will guarantee man’s success in this world and the next, for a sound human mentality can only be one which is in harmony with the rest of the world and in complete accord with the vaster system of the cosmos.

**Knowledge and guidance.**

Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. Only God can truly tell us what He is in His Being and in His attributes. And He has made this so clear in His Book, that any reader who is eager for knowledge of Him will certainly gain enlightenment from it. Again, it is only God who can truly give guidance to man. The right course of action for man can be determined only by a Being who has not only known man from his birth to his death, but also knows what has gone before his birth and what will happen after his death. It is only God who has the power and the knowledge to ordain what it befits human beings to strive for in the present world. This being so, the only realistic approach for man is to trust in His Maker and accept and follow His guidance wholeheartedly and with full confidence.

The verse takes Allah’s complete knowledge from the heavens and earth to the beginning of every human life. “He is the One Who shapes you in the wombs of your mothers as He wills” describes each person as formed by Allah before anyone can see or know the details of that life. Difference in form, sex, appearance, strength, and condition is not outside His will or knowledge. The verse does not describe people as self-made beings who came into existence by their own power. It directs them to the One who gives form in the womb. “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Almighty, All-Wise” draws the conclusion from this act of creation. The One who forms human beings and knows their hidden beginning has no partner in the right to worship. The names “the Almighty, All-Wise” close with power and wisdom. Allah has the power to create as He wills, and His creation is not without wisdom. The verse speaks after the statement that nothing is hidden from Allah. The womb, hidden from human sight, is one sign that His knowledge and power reach what people cannot control. It also prepares the discussion of revelation and right interpretation by grounding the reader in the difference between the Creator and the created. A person who has been formed by Allah is not independent of Him, and the One who creates with power and wisdom alone deserves worship.

The verse explains that the Book contains verses with different kinds of expression and teaches the right response to both. “He is the One Who has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book” begins with Allah as the giver of the Quran. “Of which some verses are precise—they are the foundation of the Book” names verses whose meaning is clear and which give the Book its firm basis. They are the place to which a reader returns when understanding other passages. “While others are elusive” names verses whose full meaning is not open in the same way. “Those with deviant hearts follow the elusive verses seeking ˹to spread˺ doubt through their ˹false˺ interpretations” describes a wrong approach: leaving the clear foundation and using an elusive expression to create confusion. “But none grasps their ˹full˺ meaning except Allah” sets a limit around what a person can claim to know. “As for those well-grounded in knowledge, they say, ‘We believe in this ˹Quran˺—it is all from our Lord’” gives the response of people firmly grounded in knowledge. They do not divide the Book against itself or use one part to deny another. “But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason” closes by asking for an attentive mind. The verse does not make the unclear a reason to ignore the Quran. It gives the clear verses their central place, directs the reader away from false interpretation, and teaches faith and humility before what Allah has kept fully within His knowledge. The distinction between the two kinds of verses protects the reader from two errors. One is to ignore the clear foundation of the Book while chasing an expression that can be bent toward a desired claim. The other is to assume that faith means pretending to know every unseen reality in full. The verse gives another way: clear verses guide belief and action, elusive verses are received with faith, and all of the Book is known to come from the same Lord. This makes knowledge a source of humility rather than a tool for spreading doubt. A reader can study, reflect, and seek the best understanding without turning limited human language into a claim to possess what Allah has kept within His own full knowledge. People of reason do not set one part of the Quran against another. They allow what is clear to provide the firm basis, and they respond to what is elusive with faith in Allah and care in interpretation. This is the discipline of knowledge: trust the Book, use its clear foundation, and leave full knowledge of what is hidden to Allah.

**Precise verses and the foundation of the Book.**

He it is Who revealed to you the Book wherein are verses that are clear lucid in proof forming the Mother Book the original basis for rulings and others allegorical whose meanings are not known such as the opening verses of some sūras. Muhkamat is the name of verses the meaning of which is open and clear to one who knows the rules of Arabic grammar fairly well. Allah Almighty has called the first kind of verses, that is, the Muhkamat Umm al-Kitab ' (which has been translated literally as 'mother verses') meaning thereby that such verses are the very root and essence of all teachings, and the meanings and explanations of which are free of doubt or ambiguity. In it are verses that are entirely clear, they are the foundations of the Book; and others not entirely clear. (He it is Who hath revealed unto thee (Muhammad) the Scripture) who sent you Gabriel with the Scripture (wherein are clear revelations) expositing the lawful and unlawful which are not abrogated and which are acted upon. (They are the substance of the Book) they are the foundation of the Book as they are the leading theme in each book. O Prophet, He is the One Who revealed to you the Qur’ān, which contains verses with clear and unambiguous meaning, and these represent the majority of the Book and are the reference point when there is disagreement. He it is who has sent down upon thee the Book, wherein are firm verses, which are the mother of the Book, and others ambiguous. Wherein are firm verses, which are the mother of the Book, and others ambiguous.

**Elusive verses and their full meaning.**

He it is Who revealed to you the Book wherein are verses that are clear lucid in proof forming the Mother Book the original basis for rulings and others allegorical whose meanings are not known such as the opening verses of some sūras. He God refers to the whole Qur’ān as 1 ‘clear’ muhkam where He says A Book whose verses have been made clear Q. 111 meaning that it contains no imperfections; and as 2 ‘allegorical’ mutashābih where He says A Book consimilar Q. 3923 meaning that its parts resemble each other in terms of beauty and veracity. Through this verse, Allah Almighty has put an end to these doubts by saying that such expressions are in the category of Mutashabihat where the outward meaning is not intended; they are, rather, a secret between Allah and His Messenger, the reality of which cannot become manifest to others for whom it is not even appropriate to go about determining the possible meanings of these words. Since the exact intention of the second kind of verses, that is, the Mutashabihat remains ambiguous and uncertain, therefore, the correct method of their interpretation would be to harmonize them with the first kind, that is, the Muhkamat . So as for those in whose hearts there is a deviation (from the truth) they follow (only) that which is not entirely clear thereof, seeking Al-Fitnah, and seeking its Ta'wil, but none knows its Ta'wil except Allah. " He also said, "As for the unclear Ayat, they can (but must not) be altered and changed, and this is a test from Allah to the servants, just as He tested them with the allowed and prohibited things. (And others (which are) allegorical) vague in their meanings to the Jews, like the use of the letters of the alphabet according to their numerical value (hisab al-Jumal) in such instances as Alif. (None knoweth its explanation) the future of this nation (save Allah). It also contains other verses that may have more than one meaning and are puzzling for most people. No one knows the true meaning of such verses besides Allah. The second relate to the unknown world (for man) and cannot, therefore, be expressed in everyday language. That is why they are framed in an allegorical style.

**Deviant hearts, doubt, and false interpretation.**

As for those in whose hearts is deviation inclination away from truth they follow the allegorical part desiring sedition among the ignorant of them throwing them into specious arguments and confusion and desiring its interpretation its explanation and none knows its interpretation its explanation save God Him alone. The Christians then expressed their doubts about some words of the Holy Qur'an in which Sayyidna 'Isa i.e. Jesus Christ has been called 'Ruhullah ' (the Spirit of Allah) or 'Kalimatullah ' (the Word of Allah), which according to them led to prove that Sayyidna Isa had a share in the divinity of Allah. Through this verse, Allah Almighty has put an end to these doubts by saying that such expressions are in the category of Mutashabihat where the outward meaning is not intended; they are, rather, a secret between Allah and His Messenger, the reality of which cannot become manifest to others for whom it is not even appropriate to go about determining the possible meanings of these words. Then, the rule is that any interpretation of the Mutashabihat which goes against the first kind should be rejected absolutely and only that interpretation should be given credence which is not against the verses of established meaning (Muhkamat). Now, if someone closes his eyes towards all these verses which have an established meaning and unnecessarily coils with the expressions, (the Word of Allah) and ‌ (a spirit from Him) and their likes from the category of Mutashabihat (verses whose definite meanings cannot be ascertained) and starts deducing from them meanings which are against the Muhkamat of Qur'an and other consistent statements, then, that would be a simple case of going astray and being ob-stinate. So as for those in whose hearts there is a deviation (from the truth) they follow (only) that which is not entirely clear thereof, seeking Al-Fitnah, and seeking its Ta'wil, but none knows its Ta'wil except Allah. (they follow that which is not entirely clear thereof) meaning, they refer to the Mutashabih, because they are able to alter its meanings to conform with their false interpretation since the wordings of the Mutashabihat encompass such a wide area of meanings. (When you see those who follow what is not so clear of the Qur'an, then they are those whom Allah described, so beware of them.)" (But those) the Jews Ka'b Ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy Ibn Akhtab and Judayy Ibn Akhtab (in whose hearts is doubt) scepticism, opposition and deviance from guidance (pursue, forsooth, that which is allegorical seeking) in the Qur'an ((to cause) dissension) pursuing disbelief, ascribing partners to Allah, and holding fast to the error they are in (by seeking to explain it) to determine the future of this nation so that dominion reverts back to them. Those who seek other than the truth leave the clear verses and focus on the unclear ones, trying to create doubts and mislead people, and interpret them to suit their corrupt views. Those who do not understand this difference fall into the error of interpreting allegorical verses quite literally. This will only lead man astray; he will never arrive at the truth.

**Well-grounded knowledge and faith.**

And those firmly rooted established and capable in knowledge al-rāsikhūna fī’l-‘ilm is the subject the predicate of which is what follows say ‘We believe in it the allegorical part that it is from God and we do not know its meaning; all of the clear and the allegorical is from our Lord’; yet none remembers yadhdhakkar the initial tā’ of yatadhakkar has been assimilated with the dhāl that is none is admonished but people of pith possessors of intellect who when they see those following that allegorical part only also say. Who are the ones 'well grounded' in knowledge as identified towards the end of the verse ‌ ? (say: "We believe in it") If the word Ta'wil means the second meaning, that is, explaining and describing, such as what Allah said,. This is because the scholars have general knowledge in, and understand what they were addressed with, even though they do not have knowledge of the true reality of things. (We believe in it) means, they believe in the Mutashabih. This is because they both are from Allah and nothing that comes from Allah is ever met by contradiction or discrepancy. (And those who are of sound instruction) those who have a sound grasp of the knowledge of the Torah: 'Abdullah Ibn Salam and his fellow companions (say: We believe therein) in the Qur'an; (the whole is from our Lord) Allah has revealed both those verses which are clear and those which are ambiguous; (but only men of understanding) who have sound minds such as 'Abdullah Ibn Salam and his fellow companions (really heed) take admonition from the simile of the Qur'an. Those who are firm in knowledge say, ‘We have faith in the entire Qur’ān because it is all from Allah’. They interpret the unclear verses according to the clear ones.

**People of reason and attention.**

And those firmly rooted established and capable in knowledge al-rāsikhūna fī’l-‘ilm is the subject the predicate of which is what follows say ‘We believe in it the allegorical part that it is from God and we do not know its meaning; all of the clear and the allegorical is from our Lord’; yet none remembers yadhdhakkar the initial tā’ of yatadhakkar has been assimilated with the dhāl that is none is admonished but people of pith possessors of intellect who when they see those following that allegorical part only also say. This is because they both are from Allah and nothing that comes from Allah is ever met by contradiction or discrepancy. Only those who have sound minds pay attention to this. There are two kinds of subjects dealt with in the Quran, one pertaining to the known human world, like historical events, signs from the universe and commandments for worldly life; the other pertaining to unseen matters which are not comprehensible by man in this life, for instance, God’s attributes, and the states of Heaven and Hell, etc. The first are clear revelations, quite precise in their meaning, since they have been couched in a direct style. Whereas a ‘human hand’ may be precisely understood, a ‘divine hand’ cannot, because of our present limited thinking capacity.
